rules.cwe_name: Generation of Predictable Numbers or Identifiers
rules.description: Tokens used for sensitive tasks, such as, password recovery, and email confirmation, should not use predictable values.
Not using `pam_acct_mgmt` after `pam_authenticate` to check the validity of a login can lead to authorization bypass.

When checking a Hash over a message, a constant-time algorithm should be used. Otherwise, an attacker may be able to forge a valid Hash for an arbitrary message by running a timing attack if they can send to the validation procedure. A successful attack can result in authentication bypass.
This reports the external APIs that are used with untrusted data, along with how frequently the API is called, and how many unique sources of untrusted data flow to it.

rules.cwe_name: Function Call with Incorrectly Specified Arguments
rules.description: Using a named argument whose name does not correspond to a parameter of the called function or method, will result in a TypeError at runtime.
Initializing SECRET_KEY of Flask application with Constant value files can lead to Authentication bypass

rules.cwe_name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Output Used by a Downstream Component ('Injection')
rules.description: Using user-controlled data to create a template can lead to remote code execution or cross site scripting.
Cookies without the `HttpOnly` attribute set can be accessed by JS scripts, making them more vulnerable to XSS attacks.

rules.cwe_name: Sensitive Cookie with Improper SameSite Attribute
rules.description: Cookies with `SameSite` set to `None` can allow for Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks.
Legacy access-control category for failures in permissions, privileges, or authorization enforcement.
Security-critical data assumed immutable can be modified by an attacker.

rules.cwe_name: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm
rules.description: Finds uses of symmetric cryptography algorithms that are weak, obsolete, or otherwise unaccepted. The key lengths allowed are 128, 192, and 256 bits. These are all the key lengths supported by AES, so any application of AES is considered acceptable.
